newsitem.title: USA: US House-Senate Republicans seek tax compromise.
newsitem.headline: US House-Senate Republicans seek tax compromise.

text.p: House and Senate Republicans tried Monday to narrow their differences on tax cut legislation in an effort to present a united front to the White House.
Their meeting was expected to last into the night, with the focus on sorting out differences in the House and Senate tax bills before Republicans meet with White House officials Tuesday.
"We're going to talk about how we proceed; then we plan on meeting with the administration tomorrow," Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi said.
"We understand where their (administration) hot spots are and we're trying to make sure they understand ours," he said.
Congressional tax negotiators met with administration officials over the weekend in an attempt to move forward on the tax bill. However, they did not resolve any key issues.
"We lost an opportunity over the weekend to make progress, and I feel very disappointed about that," Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota said.
"So over the last couple of days there has been no movement. And it increases my pessimism about our ability to ... finish our work this week," he added.
Lott offered a different assessment. "I think we're making really good progress," he said. "Tom needs to cheer up."

Lott added that he was still aiming to finish work on the tax bill before the August congressional recess. The tax legislation would implement the part of the May budget agreement between congressional leaders and the White House calling for $85 billion in net tax cuts.
The chairman of the House-Senate tax conferees urged all parties in the tax negotiations to show flexibility, citing his own proposal to scale back on a key priority.
Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, said he continued to "strongly urge that all parties involved must be flexible."
Roth said he had shown flexibility by offering to scale back proposals to expand Individual Retirement Accounts.

"If we are to come up with a tax relief bill that can pass the House and Senate and be signed by President Clinton, I would hope that others would be willing to show the same kind of flexibility," he said in a statement.
